0.title: That You May Know: The Epistle of Assurance
0.overview:
There is a letter in the New Testament that reads like the heartbeat of an old man who has seen everything and lost nothing. John — the apostle whom Jesus loved, the one who leaned against the Lord at the Last Supper, the one who stood at the foot of the cross when the others had fled — writes at the end of a long life with the urgency of a man who knows that what he carries is the most important thing in the world. He has handled the Word of Life with his own hands. He has seen the glory. And he cannot be silent.

The First Epistle of John was written to a community under assault — not from Rome, but from within. Teachers had arisen who denied the full humanity of Christ, claiming that the eternal Son had not truly come in the flesh, that the spiritual and the material could not really meet. They were sophisticated, confident, and wrong. When they left the fellowship, John writes to those who remain, not to condemn the departed but to assure the faithful: you are not the ones who have missed it. The letter is saturated with the word "know" — used over thirty times. John wants his readers to know that they have eternal life, that they are in fellowship with the Father and the Son, that the darkness is passing and the true light is already shining.

But assurance in John is never cheap. It is tested by three great evidences that run through the letter like interwoven cords: the moral test (do you walk in the light, keeping his commandments?), the social test (do you love your brothers and sisters?), and the doctrinal test (do you confess that Jesus is the Christ come in the flesh?). These are not conditions for salvation but symptoms of it — the fingerprints of new birth on a redeemed life. The person who has truly been born of God will love, will obey, and will confess. Not perfectly — John is the one who tells us that if we say we have no sin we deceive ourselves — but genuinely and persistently.

At the theological centre of the letter stands the cross. "The blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin" (1:7). "He is the propitiation for our sins" (2:2). "He laid down his life for us" (3:16). "God sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins" (4:10). John circles back to the atoning death of Christ again and again, because the cross is the ground of everything — fellowship, forgiveness, assurance, love. The love of God is not an abstraction in 1 John; it is a specific act: the sending of the Son into the world to bear the wrath that our sins deserved so that we might live through him.

The theological lens throughout this commentary is Reformed and christological, drawing especially on John Stott's The Letters of John (Tyndale New Testament Commentaries), D.A. Carson, Sinclair Ferguson, and the preaching of Alistair Begg. The governing conviction is that 1 John was written to produce settled, humble, joyful assurance in the hearts of those who have truly come to Christ — and that such assurance, far from producing complacency, is the very fire that fuels a life of love.

1.title: The Word of Life and the God of Light
1.text: <sup>1</sup>That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we looked upon and have touched with our hands, concerning the word of life — <sup>2</sup>the life was made manifest, and we have seen it, and testify to it and proclaim to you the eternal life, which was with the Father and was made manifest to us — <sup>3</sup>that which we have seen and heard we proclaim also to you, so that you too may have fellowship with us; and indeed our fellowship is with the Father and with his Son Jesus Christ. <sup>4</sup>And we are writing these things so that our joy may be complete. <sup>5</sup>This is the message we have heard from him and proclaim to you, that God is light, and in him is no darkness at all. <sup>7</sup>But if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin. <sup>8</sup>If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. <sup>9</sup>If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness. <sup>10</sup>If we say we have not sinned, we make him a liar, and his word is not in us.
1.overview:
The letter opens not with a greeting but with a declaration — the breathless, stacked-up proclamation of a man who cannot contain what he has witnessed. Four times John insists on the physicality of his testimony: heard, seen, looked upon, touched. This is no vision, no spiritual impression, no mystical encounter. The eternal Word who was with the Father before all worlds became touchable. John's hands rested on him. The Gnostic teachers who had just left the community claimed special spiritual knowledge that transcended the material. John's answer is the incarnation: the eternal life appeared, and we handled it with these hands.

From this foundation John moves to the purpose of his proclamation: fellowship — with the Father, with the Son, and with one another. And then, immediately, the first great test. The God with whom we claim fellowship is light — pure, uncompromising, all-revealing light. In him is no darkness at all. Any claim to fellowship with this God that allows a comfortable cohabitation with sin is self-deception. But the answer to sin is not despair — it is the blood of Jesus his Son, which cleanses continually (present tense) from all sin, and the promise of forgiveness to all who confess.

verseByVerse.quote: That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we looked upon and have touched with our hands, concerning the word of life
verseByVerse.commentary: The prologue of 1 John echoes the prologue of John's Gospel deliberately — "from the beginning" reaches back before creation, to the eternal pre-existence of the Son. But then comes the stunning descent: this eternal One was heard, seen, touched. John piles up the verbs of physical sensation with a kind of holy insistence, because everything depends on the reality of the incarnation. If the Son did not truly come in flesh, there is no real atonement, no real fellowship, no real salvation. The heretics John opposes were embarrassed by the material — they wanted a Christ who hovered above the physical. John will not have it. The eternal life became graspable. God became tangible. This is the scandal and the glory of the gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: That which we have seen and heard we proclaim also to you, so that you too may have fellowship with us; and indeed our fellowship is with the Father and with his Son Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary: The goal of apostolic proclamation is not information but fellowship — koinōnia, the sharing of life with God and with one another. This is the most astonishing offer in all of Scripture: that finite, sinful human beings can be brought into genuine communion with the Father and the Son. Not an audience with God, not a distant awareness of God, but fellowship — the same word used of the intimate sharing between the persons of the Trinity extended to include us. And notice that fellowship with God and fellowship with one another are inseparable: "fellowship with us... and our fellowship is with the Father." You cannot have one without the other. To be in Christ is to be in his body, and to love the Father is to love his children.

verseByVerse.quote: God is light, and in him is no darkness at all.
verseByVerse.commentary: This is one of the three great declarations of the letter — God is light (1:5), God is love (4:8, 16), God is righteous (2:29, 3:7). Light in Scripture speaks of holiness, truth, and the self-revealing glory of God. "In him is no darkness at all" — the double negative in Greek is emphatic: not any darkness, not even a shadow of moral ambiguity. This God cannot be compartmentalized. He cannot be worshipped on Sunday and accommodated to on Monday. Fellowship with this God is transformative precisely because he is what he is. Sinclair Ferguson notes that John does not say "God has light" or "God gives light" — he says God is light. His holiness is not a property he possesses; it is what he is in the depths of his being.

verseByVerse.quote: But if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin.
verseByVerse.commentary: Walking in the light does not mean sinless perfection — verse 8 immediately rules that out. It means living in the realm of transparency before God, with nothing hidden, nothing excused, nothing defended that should be confessed. And here is the glory: it is precisely in the light, where our sin is most visible, that the blood of Jesus cleanses us. The blood of Jesus does not work in the dark, where sin is denied and excused. It works in the light, where sin is acknowledged and brought to the cross. The cleansing is continuous (present tense: is cleansing) — not a one-time act at conversion but an ongoing application of the atoning blood to the ongoing failures of the walking-in-the-light believer. This is the gospel: not that we are clean, but that we are being cleansed.

verseByVerse.quote: If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
verseByVerse.commentary: Three conditional claims bracket the promise of verse 9, and they form a devastating logical trap for anyone who would deny their sinfulness. "If we say we have no sin" — self-deception, the truth is not in us. "If we say we have not sinned" — we make God a liar. Between these two lies shines the promise: if we confess — acknowledge, agree with God about — our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive. The grounds of forgiveness are not our sincerity but God's faithfulness and justice. Just — because the penalty has been paid at the cross; it would be unjust to require payment twice. Faithful — because he has promised, and he keeps his word. This is not cheap grace: it is costly grace, purchased at the highest price, offered freely to those who will stop defending themselves and start agreeing with God.

1.theology:
The Incarnation as Foundation. Everything in 1 John rests on the physical, historical, tangible reality of the incarnation. John's stacked verbs in verses 1–2 — heard, seen, looked upon, touched — are a theological rampart against every form of docetism (the heresy that Christ only appeared to be human). If Christ did not truly come in flesh, the blood shed on Calvary has no atoning value, the resurrection is a spirit's trick, and there is no real fellowship between God and humanity. The incarnation is not incidental to Christianity; it is its structural foundation. God became graspable so that we could grasp him — and through him, life.

The God Who is Light. John's declaration that "God is light, and in him is no darkness at all" has massive ethical implications. Fellowship with a God of absolute moral purity cannot coexist with a comfortable relationship with sin. The light of God is not a comfortable mood but a searching, penetrating, all-revealing reality. It is also a liberating one: in the light, where our sin is exposed, the blood of Jesus cleanses. Reformed theology has always insisted on the holiness of God as the backdrop against which the grace of God becomes luminous. You cannot appreciate the gospel without first standing in the light of who God is.
1.examples:
Then: The community John writes to had just experienced a painful split. People they had worshipped with, broken bread with, called brothers and sisters, had walked out. The departure of the false teachers left wounds and questions. Were the ones who stayed the ones who had missed the deeper truth? John's answer in chapter 1 is the apostolic testimony: we were there. We heard him, saw him, touched him. This is not speculation; it is witness. The assurance of the community rests not on their spiritual experiences but on the testimony of those who were eyewitnesses of the Word of Life.

Now: We live in a culture that treats the interior life as the truest life — feelings, impressions, spiritual experiences. The incarnation is John's counter-word: Christianity is tethered to history, to flesh, to blood, to an empty tomb. Our fellowship with God is not a feeling; it is a fact grounded in the historical reality of the Son of God made flesh. And the practice of confession — agreeing with God about what we are — is the daily discipline that keeps that fellowship living and real. Every day we come back to the same place: not to earn forgiveness, but to receive what has already been purchased.

2.title: Our Advocate, Our Obedience, Our Love
2.text: <sup>1</sup>My little children, I am writing these things to you so that you may not sin. But if anyone does sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous. <sup>2</sup>He is the propitiation for our sins, and not for ours only but also for the sins of the whole world. <sup>3</sup>And by this we know that we have come to know him, if we keep his commandments. <sup>5</sup>But whoever keeps his word, in him truly the love of God is perfected. By this we may know that we are in him: <sup>6</sup>whoever says he abides in him ought to walk in the same way in which he walked. <sup>15</sup>Do not love the world or the things in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him. <sup>16</sup>For all that is in the world — the desires of the flesh and the desires of the eyes and pride of life — is not from the Father but is from the world. <sup>17</sup>And the world is passing away along with its desires, but whoever does the will of God abides forever. <sup>24</sup>Let what you heard from the beginning abide in you. If what you heard from the beginning abides in you, then you too will abide in the Son and in the Father. <sup>25</sup>And this is the promise that he made to us — eternal life.
2.overview:
Chapter 2 moves in three great movements. First, the pastoral heart of John: he wants his readers not to sin, but he is realistic enough to know they will, and he points them to the one who stands as their advocate before the Father — Jesus Christ the righteous, the propitiation for their sins. This is the most concentrated statement of substitutionary atonement in the Johannine letters, and it is placed here, at the beginning, as the ground of all that follows.

Second, John introduces the first of his three great tests of authentic Christianity: the test of obedience. Not sinless perfection, but a life characterized by the keeping of his commandments. The person who says "I know him" but does not keep his word is a liar. Third, John warns against the love of the world — a love that competes with and displaces the love of the Father. The world and all its desires are passing away; the one who does the will of God abides forever. The chapter ends with an appeal to hold fast to what was heard from the beginning: the apostolic gospel, not the novel teaching of the antichrists who have gone out.

verseByVerse.quote: We have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous. He is the propitiation for our sins.
verseByVerse.commentary: Two words carry the whole weight of the gospel here. Paraclete — advocate, one called alongside — is the same word Jesus uses for the Holy Spirit in John 14–16. But here it is Jesus himself who is the Paraclete, standing before the Father on behalf of sinning believers. He is not merely a sympathetic observer; he is our legal representative, and he is qualified: "Jesus Christ the righteous." He can plead our case because he has fulfilled what we have not. Then the second word: propitiation — hilasmos — the averting of divine wrath by the offering of an atoning sacrifice. John does not shy away from the wrath of God. He names it and he names the answer: the Son of God himself bore what our sins deserved. Stott notes that propitiation does not mean we persuade an unwilling God to be merciful; it means the God who loved us provided at infinite cost the means by which his own justice could be satisfied and his mercy released.

verseByVerse.quote: And by this we know that we have come to know him, if we keep his commandments.
verseByVerse.commentary: The first great test of authentic Christianity is moral: does our knowing of God produce a new pattern of living? John is not teaching salvation by obedience — the advocate and the propitiation have already been established as the ground of our standing. But he is insisting that genuine faith produces genuine transformation. The person who claims to know God but whose life is characterized by ongoing, unrepentant disobedience is self-deceived. "Whoever keeps his word, in him truly the love of God is perfected" — not love for God merely, but God's love fully expressed and displayed in a human life. The model is radical: "whoever says he abides in him ought to walk in the same way in which he walked." Jesus is not just the Saviour; he is the pattern. Christlikeness is not an optional extra for the especially devout — it is the direction of every life that has been genuinely renewed.

verseByVerse.quote: “Yet I am writing you a new commandment, which is true in him and in you, because the darkness is passing away and the true light is already shining.”
verseByVerse.commentary: John describes the love commandment as simultaneously old and new — old because it has been heard from the beginning (Lev 19:18; Deut 6:5), new because it has been fulfilled and illuminated in Christ. The newness is not chronological but eschatological: something that existed before has now appeared in its fullness in the incarnate Son. “The darkness is passing away and the true light is already shining” — John's realized eschatology is striking. The new age has already dawned in Christ's coming; the old age of darkness is already being displaced, though not yet fully gone. The command to love is not a legal burden but a participation in this new world. Stott observes that the commandment becomes new each time it is obeyed, because each act of love is a fresh manifestation of the life of Christ breaking into the present.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever says he is in the light and hates his brother is still in darkness.
verseByVerse.commentary: The second great test appears here for the first time and will run through the letter: the test of love. Light and love belong together in John's world; darkness and hatred belong together. The claim to be in the light — to have fellowship with the God who is light — cannot coexist with contempt for a brother or sister. John is not describing minor personality clashes; he is describing the fundamental posture of the heart toward other members of the body of Christ. Hatred is the mark of the darkness from which we have been rescued. Love is the mark of the light into which we have been brought. And the reason is Christological: the one who walked in perfect love is the one we are called to imitate.

verseByVerse.quote: “I am writing to you, little children, because your sins are forgiven for his name’s sake.”
verseByVerse.commentary: John addresses three groups — little children, fathers, and young men — twice over (once with “I am writing,” once with “I write”), in a kind of liturgical antiphony. Whether these represent literal age groups or stages of spiritual maturity, the pastoral effect is the same: John meets each believer where they are. The “little children” have their fundamental need met — forgiveness through Christ's name. The “fathers” know him who is from the beginning — deep, seasoned, Christocentric knowledge is the mark of maturity. The “young men” have overcome the evil one and are strong, with the word of God abiding in them — active, vigorous faith that stands in the battle. Calvin notes that John's threefold assurance is itself an act of pastoral encouragement: he wants his readers to know what they have in Christ before he calls them to any duty.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not love the world or the things in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him.
verseByVerse.commentary: "The world" in John does not mean creation — God made the world and declared it good. It means the human system of values and desires organized around the self and in rebellion against God. The desires of the flesh (craving), the desires of the eyes (coveting), the pride of life (boasting) — these three cover the landscape of what the world offers and what our fallen nature reaches for. The incompatibility of world-love and Father-love is absolute: not "you must love the Father more than the world" but "the love of the Father is not in him." The two loves compete for the same space and one will always drive out the other. And the decisive argument is temporal: the world is passing away — present tense, already in process. Only the one who does the will of God abides forever.

verseByVerse.quote: “They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would have continued with us.”
verseByVerse.commentary: John names the theological moment: “it is the last hour” — realized eschatology again; the final age has arrived in Christ, and the appearance of antichrists confirms it. The antichrists (plural) are those who have seceded from the community. John's interpretation of their departure is penetrating: it was not external pressure but internal falseness that drove them out. Genuine belonging produces perseverance; those who leave demonstrate they never truly belonged. The mark of antichrist is doctrinal: denying that Jesus is the Christ (v. 22) and thereby denying the Father who sent him (v. 23). The christological confession is not optional theology — it is the hinge on which everything else turns. Sproul: “No one can claim to know the Father while denying the Son; the two stand or fall together.” The “anointing” (v. 20) from the Holy One — the Spirit's indwelling — is what keeps believers from being swept away by plausible deception.

verseByVerse.quote: Let what you heard from the beginning abide in you... And this is the promise that he made to us — eternal life.
verseByVerse.commentary: Against the novel teaching of the antichrists, John's answer is not a new revelation but a return to the beginning — to the apostolic gospel, to the original proclamation of the Word of Life. The Christian life is not a journey toward ever-more-sophisticated spiritual insight that leaves the simple gospel behind; it is a journey ever deeper into what was proclaimed from the beginning. "Let it abide in you" — the word for abide (menō) is one of John's great words, used over forty times across his Gospel and letters. The gospel is not a launching pad to be left behind; it is the atmosphere the believer breathes. And the promise embedded in that abiding is eternal life — not merely existence without end, but the life of God himself, shared with those who are in the Son.

verseByVerse.quote: “And now, little children, abide in him, so that when he appears we may have confidence and not shrink from him in shame at his coming.”
verseByVerse.commentary: John's stated purpose is to warn against those who would deceive (v. 26), but his method is not primarily polemical — it is positive: remind the readers of the Spirit's anointing (v. 27). The Holy Spirit who indwells believers “teaches you about everything” — not private new revelation, but the Spirit's illuminating work on the apostolic teaching already received. The repeated exhortation to “abide” (vv. 27, 28) is characteristic of John: remaining in Christ is both gift and calling. The eschatological horizon (v. 28) gives the command urgency: the confidence or shame experienced at Christ's appearing depends on whether one has remained in him. Verse 29 introduces a key Johannine criterion: if God is righteous, then those truly born of him will “practice righteousness.” The new birth produces a family resemblance.

2.theology:
Advocacy and Propitiation. The paired terms of 2:1–2 give us the two aspects of Christ's saving work seen from different angles. As advocate, he represents us before the Father — our case is in his hands, and he is qualified to plead it because he is righteous. As propitiation, he has already dealt with the ground of the accusation — the wrath of God against our sin has been absorbed at the cross. These are not two separate acts but two perspectives on the one act of the cross. The same sacrifice that satisfied divine justice now grounds our ongoing access to divine mercy. Reformed theology has always insisted that the atonement is both objective (propitiation — something accomplished outside us, in history, on a cross) and applied (advocacy — an ongoing ministry of Christ on our behalf). Both are necessary; together they produce the settled assurance John wants his readers to have.

The Three Tests. John's three tests — obedience (2:3–6), love (2:9–11), and belief (2:22–23) — are not a checklist for earning assurance but symptoms of new birth. Just as a doctor looks for signs of life, John looks for the signs that genuine regeneration has occurred. These tests are not meant to produce anxiety but clarity: not "have I been good enough?" but "is there genuine fruit of the Spirit in my life?" The tests are cumulative and mutually reinforcing — genuine obedience produces love; genuine love flows from right belief; genuine belief manifests in how we treat the brothers and sisters.
2.examples:
Then: The antichrists who had left the community had claimed a superior knowledge of God. Their departure seemed, to some, like the enlightened ones leaving the unenlightened behind. John's response is pastoral and pointed: the ones who left proved by their leaving that they were never truly of the community (2:19). This is not cruelty but theology — genuine new birth produces perseverance. The ones who remained, confused and perhaps diminished, were the ones who had "the anointing from the Holy One" and knew the truth (2:20). The test of authenticity is not sophistication but faithfulness to the beginning.

Now: We live in a world of novelty — new spiritualities, new therapies, new paths to self-actualization. The church is perpetually tempted to trade the apostolic gospel for something more culturally current, more psychologically satisfying, more intellectually respectable. John's word is the same: let what you heard from the beginning abide in you. The gospel does not need to be updated; it needs to be inhabited. The depth we seek is not found by moving beyond the cross — it is found by going deeper into it.

3.title: Children of God, Love in Deed
3.text: <sup>1</sup>See what kind of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God; and so we are. The reason why the world does not know us is that it did not know him. <sup>2</sup>Beloved, we are God's children now, and what we will be has not yet appeared; but we know that when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is. <sup>3</sup>And everyone who thus hopes in him purifies himself as he is pure. <sup>14</sup>We know that we have passed out of death into life, because we love the brothers. <sup>16</sup>By this we know love, that he laid down his life for us, and we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers. <sup>17</sup>But if anyone has the world's goods and sees his brother in need, yet closes his heart against him, how does God's love abide in him? <sup>18</sup>Little children, let us not love in word or talk but in deed and in truth.
3.overview:
Chapter 3 opens with one of the most arresting exclamations in all of Scripture: See what kind of love — the Greek word suggests something foreign, exotic, surprising, from another world entirely. The love that makes sinful creatures children of the holy God is not an extension of ordinary human affection. It is a different category of love altogether, an invasion from another realm. And it is not merely a legal status: "we are" — present tense, already, actually, really. The children of God are hidden to the world because the world did not recognize the Son of God either. The family resemblance is not yet complete — what we will be has not appeared — but the hope of Christlikeness at the appearing shapes the life of the believer now.

The chapter then descends from the heights of adoption to the concrete test of love: do we lay down our lives for the brothers? John defines love not by a feeling but by the cross — "he laid down his life for us" — and then applies the definition with bracing directness: if you have material resources and see a brother in need and close your heart, how does the love of God abide in you? Love in deed and truth, not in word and talk. The cross makes love costly, and costly love is the mark of those who have truly understood the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: See what kind of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God; and so we are.
verseByVerse.commentary: The word translated "see" or "behold" is an imperative of astonishment — John wants to stop his readers in their tracks and make them look at something they may have grown too familiar with. The love that produces adoption is described as foreign, exotic (potapēn) — from another country, another world. It does not belong to the natural order of things that the holy God would adopt sinful creatures as his children. And yet: "so we are." Not "so we shall be" but "so we are" — the adoption is present, actual, real. The world's failure to recognize the children of God is explained by its prior failure to recognize the Son of God. We share his hiddenness, and we will share his glory. "When he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is" — the beatific vision is transformative. To see Christ as he is will complete the work of conforming us to his image. And this hope is not passive; it purifies.

verseByVerse.quote: No one born of God makes a practice of sinning, for God's seed abides in him; and he cannot keep on sinning, because he has been born of God.
verseByVerse.commentary: This is one of the most debated passages in the New Testament, because it seems to claim sinless perfection for the believer — which 1:8 has already denied. The resolution lies in the Greek: John is speaking of the habitual, continuous practice of sin (present tense throughout). The one born of God does not live in sin as in a home, does not practice it as a settled trade. "God's seed abides in him" — the new nature implanted by the Spirit is incompatible with a life dominated by sin. This is not perfectionism; it is regeneration. The Christian still sins (1:8–9) but sin has lost its lordship. The direction of the life has been decisively reversed by the new birth, even if the journey is not yet complete. Stott calls this the "contrariety" between the old nature and the new — they are in permanent conflict, and the new is winning.

verseByVerse.quote: “By this it is evident who are the children of God, and who are the children of the devil: whoever does not practice righteousness is not of God, nor is the one who does not love his brother.”
verseByVerse.commentary: John draws the diagnostic clearly: the children of God are known by their practice of righteousness and their love for fellow believers; those without these marks belong to a different family. The example of Cain (v. 12) is sobering — his murder of Abel was not random violence but the expression of a nature: “his own deeds were evil and his brother's righteous.” Darkness hates light instinctively. This explains why the world hates believers (v. 13) — not because Christians are odd or offensive, but because righteousness exposes unrighteousness and evokes hostility. Ferguson notes that John is not teaching sinless perfectionism but the pattern and direction of a life: the regenerate person is marked by a practice (habitual walk) of righteousness, not by occasional righteous acts. The family resemblance to God or to the devil is shown in the settled orientation of the life.

verseByVerse.quote: We know that we have passed out of death into life, because we love the brothers.
verseByVerse.commentary: The language of passing from death to life echoes John 5:24, where Jesus makes the same promise to those who hear and believe. Here John gives one of the clearest tests of that passage: love for the brothers. Not love for the idea of humanity, not philanthropic sentiment toward the deserving poor, but love for the specific, awkward, demanding, sometimes disappointing brothers and sisters in the body of Christ. This love is not the ground of our passing from death to life — the cross is that ground — but it is the evidence. The one who does not love remains in death (v. 14b). The one who hates a brother is a murderer (v. 15). John does not soften this. The presence of love for the brothers and sisters is one of the clearest marks that the life of God has truly taken root in a human soul.

verseByVerse.quote: “Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer, and you know that no murderer has eternal life abiding in him.”
verseByVerse.commentary: John echoes the Sermon on the Mount (Matt 5:21–22): hatred in the heart constitutes murder at the level of the will and desire. The logic is consistent with John's characteristic moral realism — inner dispositions matter as much as outward acts, because they disclose the nature of the soul. “No murderer has eternal life abiding in him” does not mean that a true believer can never struggle with sinful anger, but that settled, cherished hatred toward a brother is incompatible with the regenerate life. The one who hates has already made the choice of Cain. Keller observes that this verse is deeply pastoral: it calls believers to examine not just their behavior but the affections that govern it, and to bring even the hidden heart before the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: By this we know love, that he laid down his life for us, and we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers.
verseByVerse.commentary: John does not define love by a feeling, a philosophy, or a sentiment. He defines it by an event: the laying down of the life of the Son of God. The cross is John's dictionary entry for love. And then, immediately, the application: "we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers." The same verb, the same construction — as he, so we. The cross is not just the means of our salvation; it is the pattern of our calling. And lest this seem too dramatic to be daily, John brings it immediately to earth: if you have the world's goods and see a brother in need and close your heart, how does God's love abide in you? The martyrdom of the cross becomes the small deaths of opening a closed hand, a closed door, a closed heart. Love in deed and truth, not word and talk.

verseByVerse.quote: By this we shall know that we are of the truth and reassure our heart before him; for whenever our heart condemns us, God is greater than our heart, and he knows everything.
verseByVerse.commentary: Here John addresses the believer whose conscience is not easily quieted — the one who loves in deed and truth and yet still wonders. The reassurance is not "your heart will eventually feel better" but something far stronger: "God is greater than our heart, and he knows everything." Our conscience is an important but imperfect instrument. It condemns us with partial knowledge. God knows everything — including the secret motions of grace in us, the genuine love that our doubting heart cannot fully see, the reality of the new birth that our feelings obscure. To appeal from our condemning heart to the all-knowing God is not presumption; it is faith. He knows us better than we know ourselves, and he has given his Son for us. This is the foundation of settled assurance.

3.theology:
Adoption and Transformation. The doctrine of adoption — huiothesia — is one of the richest in the New Testament, and 3:1–3 is one of its highest expressions. To be called children of God is not a metaphor of religious devotion; it is a declaration of a new ontological status. We have been brought into the family of God — not as servants, not as subjects, but as children who share in the inheritance of the Son. And adoption in John is both present reality ("so we are," v.1) and future consummation ("what we will be has not yet appeared," v.2). The "not yet" of our glorification does not undermine the "already" of our adoption; the hope of the appearing purifies the life of the one who holds it.

Love Defined by the Cross. John's definition of love in verse 16 is one of the most consequential sentences in the New Testament. He does not say "God is love, therefore love is whatever feels loving." He says love is defined by a specific act: the laying down of the life of the Son. The cross is love's definition, love's measure, and love's demand. Reformed theology has always insisted that the love of God is not sentimentality but holy self-giving at infinite cost. Every theology of love that avoids the cross will eventually become a theology of tolerance — and tolerance is not love. Love is the cross, and the cross makes demands.
3.examples:
Then: The community John writes to had experienced the pain of betrayal — people they had loved had left. The temptation in such a situation is to turn inward, to protect the heart, to love in word only and keep the real self safely guarded. John's word to them is the cross: he laid down his life. Not as an inspiration to imitate from a safe distance, but as the very definition and pattern of what love is. The ones who remained in the fellowship were called to love one another with an openness that made them vulnerable — precisely because that is what love, defined by the cross, requires.

Now: We live in a therapeutic culture that defines love primarily as acceptance and validation. John defines it as sacrifice. The question is not "do I feel warmly toward my brother?" but "am I laying anything down for my brother?" The test of love is not interior but behavioural — not word and talk but deed and truth. A closed hand toward a brother in need, whatever feelings accompany it, is not love in John's sense. The cross makes love costly, specific, and concrete.

4.title: Testing the Spirits and the Love of God
4.text: <sup>1</sup>Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God, for many false prophets have gone out into the world. <sup>2</sup>By this you know the Spirit of God: every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God, <sup>7</sup>Beloved, let us love one another, for love is from God, and whoever loves has been born of God and knows God. <sup>8</sup>Anyone who does not love does not know God, because God is love. <sup>9</sup>In this the love of God was made manifest among us, that God sent his only Son into the world, so that we might live through him. <sup>10</sup>In this is love, not that we have loved God but that he loved us and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins. <sup>18</sup>There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear. For fear has to do with punishment, and whoever fears has not been perfected in love. <sup>19</sup>We love because he first loved us.
4.overview:
Chapter 4 begins with a warning and ends with a declaration, and between them lies the most concentrated exposition of the love of God in the New Testament. The warning: test the spirits, for not every spirit that claims to be from God is from God. The test is doctrinal — does the spirit confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh? The incarnation is the fault line between truth and error, between the Spirit of God and the spirit of antichrist. Every age has its sophisticated spiritualities that try to have God without the incarnation, the cross without the propitiation, love without the costly sacrifice of the Son. John's answer is always the same: go back to the flesh, go back to the blood, go back to what was from the beginning.

Then, from verse 7, the chapter soars. Three times John says "God is love" (vv. 8, 16) — not "God is loving" but "God is love," love as the very essence of who he is. But he never lets this become abstraction. The love of God is immediately defined by its supreme expression: the sending of the Son to be the propitiation for our sins. And the love of God, so defined, demands a response — not fear, which has to do with punishment, but the freedom of those who know that the punishment has been absorbed, the debt paid, the wrath of God fully satisfied in the beloved Son.

verseByVerse.quote: Test the spirits to see whether they are from God, for many false prophets have gone out into the world.
verseByVerse.commentary: Spiritual experience, however powerful, is not self-validating. John's command to test the spirits is a bracing corrective to any Christianity that values experience over truth. The spirits must be tested, and the test is doctrinal: does the spirit confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh? The Greek implies an ongoing confession — not a one-time creedal assent but a settled, consistent acknowledgment of the full humanity of the incarnate Son. The spirit that refuses or undermines this confession is the spirit of antichrist. John's readers already know this is at work in the world. The discernment required is not cynicism — it is faithfulness to the apostolic testimony. Every new spiritual movement must be held against the rule: does it confess the flesh-and-blood incarnation of the Son of God?

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever loves has been born of God and knows God. Anyone who does not love does not know God, because God is love.
verseByVerse.commentary: The logic is unbreakable: if God is love by nature, then to know God is necessarily to be changed in the direction of love. You cannot truly encounter the God who is love and remain loveless. This is not an argument for universalism — many encounter the concept of God and are unchanged. It is an argument for the transforming power of genuine regeneration. The one who has been "born of God" has been given a share in the very nature of God, and the nature of God is love. The absence of love, therefore, is not merely a moral failing — it is evidence that something fundamental has not happened. John does not say "whoever does not love needs to try harder." He says "whoever does not love does not know God." The issue is not effort but encounter.

verseByVerse.quote: In this is love, not that we have loved God but that he loved us and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins.
verseByVerse.commentary: This is perhaps the most precise definition of love in all of Scripture. John corrects a natural assumption: that love begins with our response to God, our reaching toward him, our devotion and worship. No — love begins with God. It is his initiative, his descent, his gift. And it is defined not by its warmth but by its cost: the sending of the only Son to be the propitiation for our sins. D.A. Carson calls this "the love of God at the cross" — not the cross as the evidence that we are lovable, but the cross as the evidence that God is love. We were not lovable; we were under wrath. Into that situation, at the cost of the Son, love came. The Christian's love for others is always a response to and a reflection of this prior, costly, initiative-taking love of God.

verseByVerse.quote: “Beloved, if God so loved us, we also ought to love one another.”
verseByVerse.commentary: The logic of grace is unmistakable: we love because we have first been loved (cf. 4:19). The “if” is not hypothetical but factual — “since God so loved us.” The love poured out in Christ's atoning death is both the motive and the pattern for horizontal love. Verse 12 offers a startling theological claim: “No one has ever seen God” — yet when believers love one another, “God abides in us and his love is perfected in us.” The invisible God becomes visible through the community of love. The church's love is not merely a moral imperative but a theo-logical act: it is the medium through which God's own love reaches its telos. Stott: “Love for our brothers and sisters is the only way in which the invisible God becomes visible.”

verseByVerse.quote: So we have come to know and to believe the love that God has for us. God is love, and whoever abides in love abides in God, and God abides in him.
verseByVerse.commentary: "We have come to know and to believe" — both verbs together, neither alone. Knowledge without belief remains cold; belief without knowledge has no stable object. Together they produce abiding — the settled, ongoing mutual indwelling of the believer and the God who is love. "God abides in him" — this is not a feeling but a reality, as solid as the resurrection, as sure as the promise of the one who cannot lie. The one who abides in love — who lives in the posture of receiving and extending the love of God — abides in God himself. This is the mystical union that John's Gospel calls the vine and the branches, and here it is tethered to the most practical expression: love for one another.

verseByVerse.quote: “By this is love perfected with us, so that we may have confidence for the day of judgment, because as he is so also are we in this world.”
verseByVerse.commentary: One of the most stunning declarations in the epistle: the believer's standing before the judgment seat is grounded in union with Christ — “as he is so also are we in this world.” Not as he was, but as he is: the exalted, glorified Christ in whom the believer is hidden (Col 3:3). The confidence (parrēsia) we have now in prayer anticipates the confidence of the final day. Mature love — love that has been “perfected” or brought to its intended goal — casts out fear (v. 18) precisely because it rests not on our performance but on Christ's. Sproul notes that this is not presumption but assurance grounded in the work of another: the righteousness of Christ credited to the believer is the basis of fearless standing before God.

verseByVerse.quote: There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear... We love because he first loved us.
verseByVerse.commentary: Fear and love are incompatible in the realm of relationship with God. The fear John speaks of is the cringing, punitive terror of one who expects condemnation — the fear of one who has not understood that the propitiation has already been made, the wrath already absorbed, the judgment already borne by the Son. Perfect love — the complete, mature love of God fully received and rested in — leaves no room for this fear. It is cast out, expelled, driven away. This is not a command to try harder to feel less afraid; it is a description of what happens when the love of God is truly known and believed. And then, the simplest and most beautiful verse in the chapter: "We love because he first loved us." Our love is not original; it is responsive. It is an echo of a prior Voice. All the love we extend — to God, to one another — is borrowed capital from the inexhaustible treasury of the God who is love.

verseByVerse.quote: “If anyone says, ‘I love God,’ and hates his brother, he is a liar; for he who does not love his brother whom he has seen cannot love God whom he has not seen.”
verseByVerse.commentary: John's epistle reaches a sharp climax here. The vertical claim — “I love God” — is measured by the horizontal reality. The visible brother is the test of the invisible God. If the love of God has not produced the capacity to love a concrete, flawed, visible person, the claim to love God is simply false. The argument moves from the lesser to the greater: if you cannot love one you can see, you certainly do not love One you cannot see. Verse 21 grounds this inseparability in the divine commandment itself — God has ordered these two loves as one. Keller observes that John is not reducing love for God to social ethics; rather, genuine theological knowledge of who God is and what he has done invariably produces the kind of love for others that crosses social barriers and costs something.

4.theology:
God is Love. The statement "God is love" (vv. 8, 16) is one of the most misused sentences in Scripture. It is taken to mean that love is God — that whatever we call love must be divine, that God must approve of whatever we name as love. John means the opposite: God defines love, not the other way around. And he defines it immediately by a specific act: the sending of the Son to be the propitiation. To say "God is love" in John's sense is to say that God, in his innermost being, is the kind of God who sends his only Son into the world to die for sinners who could not save themselves. That is the love John is talking about. It is not soft; it is costly. It is not tolerant; it is propitiatory. It is not vague; it has flesh and blood and a cross and an empty tomb.

The Expulsion of Fear. The pastoral application of the doctrine of propitiation in verses 17–18 is one of the most comforting passages in the New Testament. The believer who is tortured by fear of God's judgment has not yet fully grasped what the propitiation means: that the very wrath they fear has been exhausted, absorbed, satisfied in the beloved Son. Perfect love casts out fear not by denying the reality of judgment but by pointing to the one who bore it. Reformed theology speaks of the "double jeopardy" of the cross: it would be unjust for God to punish twice what Christ has already borne. The blood of Jesus is the answer to every accusing conscience, every fear of condemnation, every midnight terror of a soul that wonders whether it is safe with God.
4.examples:
Then: The community had been shaken by teachers who claimed spiritual authority and offered a more sophisticated understanding of God. The test John gives is arrestingly simple: do they confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh? Not "do they seem spiritual?" Not "do they have impressive experiences?" But: do they hold to the incarnation? This is always the fault line. Every theological error that has ever devastated a church has at some point compromised either the full deity or the full humanity of Christ. John's readers are given a test simple enough for a child and decisive enough to unmask every false spirit.

Now: "We love because he first loved us" is the answer to every form of Christian guilt and striving. The Christian life is not a performance of love in order to earn God's approval; it is a response of love to a love already given, already completed, already victorious at the cross. When love runs dry — as it will — the answer is not to try harder but to go back to the source: "In this is love, not that we have loved God..." The spring of all Christian love is the love of God in the cross of his Son. Drink there again, and love will flow.

5.title: Faith that Overcomes, Life that is Sure
5.text: <sup>1</sup>Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God, and everyone who loves the Father loves whoever has been born of him. <sup>4</sup>For everyone who has been born of God overcomes the world. And this is the victory that has overcome the world — our faith. <sup>5</sup>Who is it that overcomes the world except the one who believes that Jesus is the Son of God? <sup>11</sup>And this is the testimony, that God gave us eternal life, and this life is in his Son. <sup>12</sup>Whoever has the Son has life; whoever does not have the Son of God does not have life. <sup>13</sup>I write these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, that you may know that you have eternal life. <sup>20</sup>And we know that the Son of God has come and has given us understanding, so that we may know him who is true; and we are in him who is true, in his Son Jesus Christ. This is the true God and eternal life.
5.overview:
The final chapter of 1 John brings the letter to its great crescendo. The three tests — belief, love, obedience — converge in a single declaration: everyone born of God overcomes the world, and the victory is faith. Not faith as a heroic human achievement, but faith as the empty hand that receives the Son of God — and in receiving the Son, receives life itself. "Whoever has the Son has life; whoever does not have the Son of God does not have life." The whole letter has been building to this clarity: salvation is not a process, not a feeling, not a spiritual achievement. It is a person. To have the Son is to have life. To be without the Son is to be without life. There is no middle ground.

And then, the stated purpose of the letter, which makes it the most explicitly pastoral book in the New Testament: "I write these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, that you may know that you have eternal life." Not that you may hope, or that you may feel, or that you may occasionally experience. That you may know. The epistle of assurance reaches its goal: settled, humble, grateful certainty in the hearts of those who have the Son. The letter closes with the most luminous declaration of all — "This is the true God and eternal life" — Jesus Christ himself, the content of the eternal life that John has been proclaiming from the beginning, the one who was with the Father and was manifested to us, in whom and through whom and for whom all things are.

verseByVerse.quote: This is the victory that has overcome the world — our faith.
verseByVerse.commentary: The Christian's relationship to the world has been a thread throughout the letter — do not love the world (2:15), the world did not know the Father (3:1), the spirit of antichrist is in the world (4:3). Now John declares the decisive verdict: the world has been overcome. The tense is significant — "has overcome" is perfect, completed action with ongoing results. The decisive victory was won at the cross, where the ruler of this world was cast out (John 12:31). The believer's faith does not win the victory; it appropriates a victory already won. And the content of that faith is specified: "Jesus is the Son of God." Not a bare intellectual assent, but a living trust in the one who is both fully human (Jesus) and fully divine (the Son of God). This is the faith that overcomes, because this is the faith that rests on the Overcomer.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever has the Son has life; whoever does not have the Son of God does not have life.
verseByVerse.commentary: The three witnesses — water, blood, Spirit — have been variously interpreted, but the most compelling reading connects them to the ministry of Jesus: water (his baptism, where the Father declared him the beloved Son), blood (his death, where he bore the sins of the world), and Spirit (the ongoing testimony of the Holy Spirit to the truth of what the water and blood signify). Against the heretics who accepted the baptism but denied the atoning death, John insists: both the water and the blood bear witness. The Spirit witnesses within the believer to the truth of this testimony. And the conclusion is one of the starkest in all of Scripture: life is in the Son, and only in the Son. To have the Son is to have life. To be without the Son is to be without life. This is not religious exclusivism; it is ontological necessity. Life is a person, and his name is Jesus.

verseByVerse.quote: I write these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, that you may know that you have eternal life.
verseByVerse.commentary: This is the purpose statement of the entire letter, and it is breathtaking in its pastoral ambition. John writes not to produce uncertainty, not to keep his readers anxiously examining themselves for signs of genuine faith, but to produce knowledge — settled, sure, confident knowledge that they have eternal life. The parallel with John 20:31 is instructive: the Gospel was written that readers might believe; the letter was written that believers might know. The letter is the epistle of assurance. All three tests — moral, social, doctrinal — have been applied not to condemn but to confirm, not to produce despair but to produce certainty. The Christian who has read this letter carefully and found in themselves the fruit of new birth — love, obedience, right belief — can say with John: I know that I have eternal life. Not "I hope" or "I think" or "I'm fairly confident." I know.

verseByVerse.quote: This is the confidence that we have toward him, that if we ask anything according to his will he hears us.
verseByVerse.commentary: The assurance of eternal life produces a correlate confidence: boldness in prayer. The one who knows they have the Son knows they have access to the Father. The condition — "according to his will" — is not a limiting escape clause but a liberating one. To pray according to God's will is not to pray in uncertainty but in the deepest possible confidence, because God's will is the will of the one who sent his Son for us, who loves us with an everlasting love, who is working all things together for the good of those who love him. John then gives a specific example: praying for a sinning brother. The community of love looks out for one another — not just in material need but in spiritual danger. We intercede for the one who is wandering, and God hears.

verseByVerse.quote: We know that the Son of God has come and has given us understanding, so that we may know him who is true; and we are in him who is true, in his Son Jesus Christ. This is the true God and eternal life.
verseByVerse.commentary: The letter closes with three great certainties introduced by "we know" — the verb that has tolled through the letter like a bell. We know that everyone born of God does not keep on sinning. We know that we are from God and the whole world lies in the power of the evil one. We know that the Son of God has come. These three certainties — about the new birth, about the two kingdoms, about the coming of the Son — are the pillars of Christian assurance. And the final declaration may be the most exalted sentence in the letter: "This is the true God and eternal life." The antecedent of "this" is Jesus Christ — the Son who has come, who has given us understanding, in whom we are. He is the true God. He is eternal life. The letter that began with the Word of Life ends with the same proclamation: life is a person, the eternal Son, who was with the Father and was manifested to us — and whom to know is life everlasting.

5.theology:
Faith as Victory. The declaration of 5:4 — "this is the victory that has overcome the world — our faith" — is one of the most important statements about the nature of faith in Scripture. Faith is not a spiritual achievement, a heightened state of consciousness, or a moral virtue we cultivate. It is a hand that receives, a trust that rests, a confidence that looks away from itself to the Son of God who has already overcome. The perfect tense — "has overcome" — points to the finished work of Christ at the cross as the source and ground of the believer's victory. We do not overcome the world by spiritual heroism; we overcome it by trusting the one who already has.

Assurance as Gift. The stated purpose of the letter — "that you may know that you have eternal life" (5:13) — stands as a rebuke to every theology that treats Christian assurance as presumption or spiritual pride. John writes to produce certainty. Reformed theology has always distinguished between assurance and presumption: presumption claims safety without evidence; assurance rests on the testimony of the Spirit, the evidence of new birth, and the promises of God. The three tests of the letter are not meant to produce anxiety but confirmation — the gentle hand of a faithful pastor showing the believer where the signs of life are visible. To know that you have eternal life is not arrogance; it is the appropriate response to the faithfulness of the God who cannot lie.
5.examples:
Then: The community, battered by false teaching and painful departure, needed to know one thing above all: that they had not missed it, that they were in the Son, that the life they had received was real and was eternal. John writes to give them that certainty — not a new experience, not a higher spirituality, but the settled confidence of those who have the Son and therefore have life. The simplicity of the final verdict — "whoever has the Son has life" — is both the most inclusive and most exclusive statement possible: inclusive, because anyone may have the Son; exclusive, because there is no life outside of him.

Now: In an age of therapeutic Christianity, where the goal is often feeling good about ourselves, John's letter is a corrective and a comfort. Assurance in John is not a feeling to be cultivated; it is a knowledge to be received — grounded in the testimony of God himself (5:9–10), confirmed by the evidence of new birth, and resting ultimately on the person of the Son. "This is the true God and eternal life" — Jesus Christ, the same yesterday, today, and forever. Whatever else may be uncertain in a Christian life, this is not: whoever has the Son has life, and the Son cannot be taken away.
